title: why monks don't beg
hookLine: a shaved head, a simple robe, a bowl at dawn: what the alms round really is

cards: Dawn in a town in Thailand or Laos. A line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot down the street, heads shaved, each carrying a covered bowl. People kneel on mats by the curb with pots of rice.
The monks don't ask for anything. And the people giving are often the ones who bow. To an outsider it can look like begging.
It isn't, and the difference is today's word.

teach.h: THE SHAVED HEAD, THE SIMPLE ROBE
teach.b: Dana means giving. Start with the monks. The shaved head and the simple robe go back to the Buddha's own leaving home: the story says he cut off his hair with his sword.
Shaving it lets go of vanity, a way of saying: I'm not dressing for anyone.

teach.h: A BOWL, A RAZOR, A NEEDLE
teach.b: Traditionally a monk owns almost nothing: robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a few small things.
In the Theravada tradition, monks don't eat after midday. That's a training rule for monastics, not a fast everyone keeps.
And their food comes from giving. So the alms round isn't begging; it's an exchange. The monk gets a meal.
The giver practices dana, which many Buddhists understand as making merit: good karma, and a lighter heart.
When the Buddha met people who'd never heard him teach, the texts say he often started with giving, before anything else.
In many East Asian monasteries, monks and nuns cook and farm for themselves, and lay people give in other ways. The open hand is the same.

how: Buddhists practice dana by offering food, robes and medicine to monks and nuns, most visibly on the morning alms round in Theravada countries and at temple meals (in Sri Lanka, families 'give a dana'), and by giving to others in daily life; some meditation teachers teach freely on a dana basis.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: monks on the alms round are begging
they don't ask. people give, and giving is a practice for the giver too.
in the Theravada tradition, monks don't eat after midday
a training rule for monastics, not a fast for everyone.
it's any giving: food, time, attention, help.

games.q: the Buddha meets someone who has never heard him teach. what does he usually talk about first, in the old accounts?
games.why: giving came first, then good conduct. the deeper teachings came once the listener was ready.

games.q: what a monk traditionally owns: build the list.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. On the first breath, notice what an open hand feels like.
On the second, think of one thing you could give that isn't money: time, attention, a kind word. On the third, picture someone receiving it.

wordCard.voice: Dana. Giving: what fills the monk's bowl, and the first practice the Buddha taught. Fifth word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, a gift. The first of the perfections (pāramī).

carryVoice: Your line: give first. In the old order of teaching, the open hand came before everything else. That's day five.
